title: "Reverse mode: the discrete adjoint"

Forward sensitivities cost one additional state vector per direction
in $\theta$, so the gradient of a scalar objective over $M$ parameters
costs $M$ times the value alone. For a scalar objective $L$, such as a
likelihood or a residual sum of squares, the transposed computation
delivers the whole gradient at a cost independent of $M$
[@griewank2008evaluating; @naumann2012art]. cppDE builds this mode with
`cppODE(..., derivMode = "reverse")`.

The reverse mode computes a contraction, not the sensitivity matrix.
Given a cotangent $w \in \mathbb{R}^{n_t \times n_x}$ on the observed
trajectory, one sweep returns
[]{#eq-adjoint-contraction}
$$
  \bar\theta_j
    = \sum_{o=1}^{n_t} \sum_{i=1}^{n_x}
      w_{oi} \,
      \frac{\partial x_i(t_o)}{\partial \theta_j},
  \qquad j = 1,\dots,n_x+n_p, \tag{22}
$$
where $o$ runs over the observation times and $i$ over the state
components. Row $o$ of $w$ is written $w_o \in \mathbb{R}^{n_x}$, the
cotangent at $t_o$. For a least-squares objective $w$ is the residual
weighted by the error model, and $\bar\theta$ is $\nabla_\theta L$
exactly. Several cotangents may be supplied as columns of a
three-dimensional array, one sweep each.

## The adjoint equation

The contraction [(22)](#eq-adjoint-contraction) can be evaluated
without forming $S_p$, the forward sensitivity of
[(12)](methods-forward.html#eq-sensitivity-p). Both backends implement the classical
construction below, with different discretisations. Define
$\lambda(t) \in \mathbb{R}^{n_x}$ backwards from the end of the
observed interval by
[]{#eq-adjoint-ode}
$$
  \dot\lambda = -J(x, p, t)^{\mathsf T}\lambda,
  \qquad \lambda(T^+) = 0,
  \qquad \lambda(t_o^-) = \lambda(t_o^+) + w_o, \tag{23}
$$
so that $\lambda$ is continuous between observation times and jumps by
the cotangent row at each. Along the solution the two Jacobian terms
cancel,
[]{#eq-adjoint-identity}
$$
  \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}
    \left(\lambda^{\mathsf T} S_p\right)
    = -\lambda^{\mathsf T} J S_p
      + \lambda^{\mathsf T}\!
        \left(J S_p + \frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\right)
    = \lambda^{\mathsf T} \frac{\partial f}{\partial p}, \tag{24}
$$
so $\lambda$ is defined without reference to $\theta$. Integrating
[(24)](#eq-adjoint-identity) over $[t_0, T]$ and collecting the jumps,
which contribute exactly the terms of [(22)](#eq-adjoint-contraction),
gives
[]{#eq-adjoint-result}
$$
  \bar\theta
    = \left(\frac{\partial x_0}{\partial \theta}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!
      \lambda(t_0)
    + \left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial \theta}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!
      \int_{t_0}^{T}
      \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!\lambda(t)\,
      \mathrm{d}t . \tag{25}
$$
When $\theta$ consists of the initial state and the parameters
themselves, both outer factors are identities and a reverse solve
reports the pair
[]{#eq-adjoint-quadrature}
$$
  \bar x_0 = \lambda(t_0),
  \qquad
  \bar p = \int_{t_0}^{T}
    \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!\lambda(t)\,
    \mathrm{d}t. \tag{26}
$$
A reparametrisation $p = \Phi(\theta)$ is applied afterwards through
the outer factors of [(25)](#eq-adjoint-result), the chain rule of
[(13)](methods-forward.html#eq-sensitivity-theta) applied on the left.

The gradient costs one backward solve of a linear system of dimension
$n_x$ and a quadrature of dimension $n_p$, whatever $M$;
$\partial f/\partial p$ enters only contracted with $\lambda$ and is
never formed. The two parts of [(26)](#eq-adjoint-quadrature) are
returned stacked in the row order of the `tangent` argument,
states first, then parameters.

## Discrete and continuous adjoints

Equation [(23)](#eq-adjoint-ode) describes the exact trajectory; cppDE
provides both common discretisations of it. The *continuous*
adjoint differentiates, then discretises: [(23)](#eq-adjoint-ode) is
solved backwards by an integrator of its own over forward states
recovered by interpolation [@cao2003adjoint]. This is the route of
CVODES, exposed by `cvode()` ([adjoint sensitivity analysis](methods-cvode.html#asa)). The
*discrete* adjoint, implemented by `cppODE()`, reverses
that order: it transposes the map the forward run applied, one
accepted step at a time. Both approximate the same gradient and
converge as the tolerance is lowered. They differ in three respects.

**Consistency of value and gradient.** The discrete adjoint
differentiates the computed trajectory and returns the derivative of
the reported value, up to rounding. The continuous adjoint approximates
the derivative of the exact solution, which no run computes, so its
gradient is consistent with the accompanying value only to
$O(\mathrm{tol})$, and tightening the backward tolerance alone does not
remove the difference.

**Discontinuities.** A jump in the state implies a jump in
$\lambda$, given by the transposed saltation matrix of the event. The
continuous adjoint restarts its backward integration with that matrix
at every event; in the discrete adjoint the jump is the transpose of
arithmetic the forward run performed, handled like any other step.

**Linear algebra per step.** The discrete adjoint of an implicit
step is one transposed solve against the step's iteration matrix,
evaluated at the checkpointed state, with neither Newton iteration nor
error control. The continuous adjoint integrates a stiff linear ODE
with its own step-size control and step count.

## The step map and its adjoint

Reverse accumulation has no counterpart in an augmented arithmetic: a
dual number holds its derivative with its value, available as soon
as an operation has executed, whereas an adjoint sums over all later
uses of a quantity. A step's adjoint is obtained either by recording
its operations on a tape and traversing it backwards, or in closed
form, since the map is one accepted step of a known method on a fixed
grid. cppDE uses the closed form and keeps no tape.

An accepted step of the multistep family decomposes into the Nordsieck
rescale and Pascal shift, the corrector, and the tail the controller
applies between the acceptance of this step and the next:
[]{#eq-step-pred}[]{#eq-step-corr}[]{#eq-step-tail}
$$
\begin{align}
  z^{\text{pred}} &= A\, z^{\text{in}}, \tag{27}\\
  r(y, z^{\text{pred}}, \theta) &= 0, \tag{28}\\
  z^{\text{out}} &= B\, z^{\text{pred}} + c\, a, \qquad a = y - z^{\text{pred}}_0. \tag{29}
\end{align}
$$
The operators $A$, $B$ and $c$ act on the slot index only; their
coefficients follow from the Nordsieck carry, the order, step-size
history and counters the stepper holds beside the slots, and are the
same for every state component. They are read off the stepper, not transposed by hand: a
probe whose states are the Nordsieck slots is driven through the
routines of the forward step, seeded with the identity in the
$[\text{slot} \times \text{component}]$ array, and one pass returns
every column. The adjoint therefore uses exactly the coefficients of
the forward step.

The corrector is differentiated by the implicit function theorem.
Since $\partial r/\partial y$ is the iteration matrix
$W = \tfrac{1}{\gamma} I - J$ the forward step factorises, one transposed solve
against $W$ replaces the Newton iteration. For the Rosenbrock family
the counterpart is a transposed stage recursion, six solves against one
factorisation; for an explicit method, the backward recursion over the
tableau.

The code generator emits the contractions the adjoint requires beside
the right-hand side: $J^{\mathsf T}\lambda$,
$(\partial f/\partial p)^{\mathsf T}\lambda$ and, for a Rosenbrock
method, the same two applied to $J v$, which contain a second derivative
because the stages solve against a matrix built from the Jacobian.

## Checkpoint per step

The forward run stores one checkpoint per accepted step: the
step-start state, the carry, the time, the step size, and a record of
the operations the controller applied to the carry afterwards. Memory
is linear in the number of steps and holds no derivatives. The
factorisations of the forward run are not kept, so the sweep re-forms
the iteration matrix $W_k$ at each checkpoint. The slot operators are
cached, keyed on the carry and the step size, so the probe runs only
where the controller changed the control state.

The transposed solve $W_k^{\mathsf T} \mu = b$ goes through the
factorisation of a later step's matrix $W_h$, which the sweep holds, by
iterative refinement,
$$
  \mu \leftarrow \mu + W_h^{-\mathsf T}\bigl(b - W_k^{\mathsf T}\mu\bigr),
  \qquad
  W_k^{\mathsf T}\mu = \tfrac{1}{\gamma}\,\mu - J_k^{\mathsf T}\mu ,
$$
until the correction is at rounding level, so the answer is that of a
direct solve. Each pass costs a pair of triangular solves and a product
with $J_k^{\mathsf T}$. A pass is cheaper than a factorisation by the
ratio of their floating-point work, which KLU reports, and the sweep
refines only while that ratio allows at least three passes; where the
iteration converges too slowly or exhausts that budget, $W_k$ is
factorised and becomes the held matrix. The budget depends on the
factors alone, so a sweep is reproducible.

Observations lie at interpolated times and are evaluated through the
continuous extension of the step containing them. The adjoint of that
evaluation comes from the same probe: after the tail, the probe holds
a valid interpolant, and evaluating it at the observation time yields
the row $\partial x_{\text{interp}} / \partial (z^{\text{pred}}, a)$
directly.

## Checkpoint reuse

The sweep reads only the checkpoints, so the forward and backward
passes can be separate calls. A reverse solve with
`keepStore = TRUE` returns its checkpoints as `$store`; a
later solve of the same model at the same times and parameters accepts
them through `store`, performs no integration and proceeds
directly to the sweep. A store created at a different parameter value
is rejected. The call that creates a store may omit the cotangent and
then performs a value-only run. A store holds its checkpoints until the
garbage collector frees it or `releaseStore()` frees them at once; a
solve given a released store integrates again.

A gradient needs two solves at the same parameter value, one for the
values from which the cotangent is formed and one for the sweep; the
store removes the second integration. The columns of a
three-dimensional cotangent sweep the one store in turn, so
$n_{\text{seed}}$ cotangents cost $n_{\text{seed}}$ sweeps and a single
integration.

Under `derivMode = "forward-reverse"` both arguments are refused:
a checkpoint of that mode holds tangents, which live in the arena of
the recording solve and do not outlive it, so every second-order sweep
is preceded by its own integration.

## The adjoint of an event {#event-adjoint}

An event is a map of its own between two steps. The forward run
transports the discontinuity with the [Heun sandwich](methods-events.html#time-triggered-events): a shift to the event surface, the resets, and a
shift back to the grid time. Each shift is taken over the residual of
the event time, which is zero in value and has only derivatives.
In value the jump is therefore a plain jump, and the sandwich reduces
to the classical saltation relation
[]{#eq-saltation}
$$
  \mathrm{d}x = R'\!\left(\mathrm{d}x_{\text{before}} + f_{\text{before}}\, s\right)
              - f_{\text{after}}\, s, \tag{30}
$$
with $R$ the resets, $R'$ their Jacobian and $s$ the differential of the
event time. For a root event $g(x, t, p) = 0$ the implicit function
theorem gives
$s = -(\nabla g \cdot \mathrm{d}x + \partial g/\partial p \cdot
\mathrm{d}p) / \dot g$; for a time-triggered event at $t = \tau(p)$,
$s = (\partial \tau/\partial p)\cdot \mathrm{d}p$.

Equation [(30)](#eq-saltation) is linear in $\mathrm{d}x_{\text{before}}$
and $\mathrm{d}p$, so its transpose can be read off. Contracting it
with a cotangent $\lambda_{\text{after}}$ and collecting the terms that
multiply $s$ leaves one scalar $\kappa$,
[]{#eq-saltation-adjoint}
$$
  \kappa = \lambda_{\text{after}}^{\mathsf T}
           \left(R' f_{\text{before}} - f_{\text{after}}\right),
  \qquad
  \lambda_{\text{before}}
    = R'^{\mathsf T}\lambda_{\text{after}}
    + \kappa \left(\frac{\partial s}{\partial x}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}, \tag{31}
$$
and the parameter cotangent additionally receives
$\kappa\,(\partial s/\partial p)^{\mathsf T}$. For a root event both
derivatives of $s$ contain the factor $-\kappa/\dot g$: the state picks up
$-(\kappa/\dot g)\nabla g$ and the parameters
$-(\kappa/\dot g)\,\partial g/\partial p$. For a time-triggered event
$\partial s/\partial x = 0$ and the parameters pick up
$\kappa\,\partial\tau/\partial p$.

The transpose $R'^{\mathsf T}$ is applied reset by reset, in reverse
order. A reset that replaces a state removes the incoming cotangent of
that component, one that adds to it leaves the cotangent unchanged, and
one that multiplies it by $h$ scales it by $h$; where $h$ depends on
the state or the parameters, its derivatives enter the same transpose.
The adjoint of a jump therefore requires the right-hand side at both
ends, $\nabla g$ and $\dot g$, and the model's derivatives of the reset
and event-time expressions, but no Jacobian of $f$: every term the two
shifts would contribute has the residual as a factor, and that
factor is zero.

After a jump the multistepper restarts: `initialize` builds the
Nordsieck history from a single state as $z_0 = x$ and
$z_1 = h\, f(x, t)$, with the remaining slots zero, so the cotangent of
the history collapses onto that state. With $\bar z_j$ the cotangent of
slot $j$, the restart contributes
[]{#eq-restart-collapse}
$$
  \bar x = \bar z_0 + h\, J^{\mathsf T} \bar z_1,
  \qquad
  \bar p = h \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\right)^{\!\mathsf T} \bar z_1, \tag{32}
$$
and slots above the first contribute nothing. The same map applies at
the start of the trajectory.

## Second order of an event's adjoint

The differential $s$ of the event time is zero in value, with
$\mathrm{d}s \neq 0$, so
[]{#eq-s-squared}
$$
  s^{2} = 0, \qquad \mathrm{d}\!\left(s^{2}\right) = 2 s\,\mathrm{d}s = 0,
  \qquad \mathrm{d}^{2}\!\left(s^{2}\right) = 2\,(\mathrm{d}s)^{2} \neq 0 , \tag{33}
$$
and terms of order $s^{2}$ drop from the gradient but not from the
Hessian. Three such terms enter a jump. The same three enter a
time-triggered event at $t = \tau(p)$, whose residual is
$s = \tau - \mathrm{scalar}(\tau)$: a time-triggered event is the same
five-stage sandwich [(39)](#eq-root-sandwich), and its transpose is that
program reversed with this $s$. The classical saltation alone is
exact in value but wrong in the tangents once the jump height moves
with a parameter, because
$\bar x_{a} = (I - s J_{a})^{\mathsf T}\bar x_{o}$ then has a second
factor that is not zero in value.

The first term is the curvature of the shift. Each half of the
sandwich is a Heun step,
[]{#eq-heun-curvature}
$$
  x_{\ast} = x_{\text{before}} + f_{\text{before}}\, s
           + \tfrac{1}{2}\, a_{\text{before}}\, s^{2},
  \qquad
  a = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} f + \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}, \tag{34}
$$
and $a\,s$ is the difference of the two right-hand sides the step
already evaluates, so no Jacobian is needed.

The second is the post-jump state, which the sweep reconstructs
because the store keeps only $x_{\text{before}}$. Rebuilt from the bare
reset it would satisfy $\partial x_{\text{after}} / \partial t^{*} = 0$,
whereas
[]{#eq-post-jump-motion}
$$
  \frac{\partial x_{\text{after}}}{\partial t^{*}}
    = f_{\text{before}} - f_{\text{after}} , \tag{35}
$$
so the reconstruction runs the sandwich, not the reset.

The third comes from the quadrature. The parameter cotangent
[]{#eq-quadrature-split}
$$
  \bar p_{k} = \int_{t_0}^{T} G_{k}\,\mathrm{d}t
             = \int_{t_0}^{t^{*}} + \int_{t^{*}}^{T},
  \qquad
  G_{k} = \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial p_{k}}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!\lambda, \tag{36}
$$
is split at $t^{*}$, where $G_{k}$ jumps with the state.
Differentiating a split integral with a moving split point leaves the
jump of the integrand at the split,
[]{#eq-quadrature-jump}
$$
  \frac{\partial \bar p_{k}}{\partial v}
  \;\supset\;
  \Big( G_{k}(t^{*-}) - G_{k}(t^{*+}) \Big)\,
  \frac{\partial t^{*}}{\partial v} . \tag{37}
$$
Only parameters whose $\partial f / \partial p_{k}$ depends on a state
the reset changed contribute.

Implemented as accumulations scaled by the residual, all three are
zero in value and hold $\partial t^{*} / \partial v$ in their tangent,
so the gradient is unchanged. For a time-triggered event at
$t = \tau(p)$ the residual is $\tau - \mathrm{scalar}(\tau)$; for a root event it is
[]{#eq-root-residual}
$$
  s = -\,\frac{g - \mathrm{scalar}(g)}{\dot g},
  \qquad
  \dot g = \frac{\partial g}{\partial t} + \nabla g \cdot f , \tag{38}
$$
read at the stored state. Localisation ignores the tangents, so that
state holds $\partial x / \partial \theta$ at a fixed time and
$\nabla g$ contracts it to the event time's.

## Transposing the root sandwich

The jump is the composition
[]{#eq-root-sandwich}
$$
  x_{e} = x_{b} + f_{b} s, \quad
  x_{\ast} = x_{b} + \tfrac{1}{2}(f_{b} + f_{e}) s, \quad
  x_{a} = R(x_{\ast}), \quad
  x_{k} = x_{a} - f_{a} s, \quad
  x_{o} = x_{a} - \tfrac{1}{2}(f_{a} + f_{k}) s , \tag{39}
$$
with $f_{e} = f(x_{e}, t^{*})$, $f_{a} = f(x_{a}, t^{*})$ and
$f_{k} = f(x_{k}, t_*^{(0)})$, $t_*^{(0)}$ the grid time. This
straight-line program is transposed assignment by assignment, not through a collected closed form: a
collected form pruned by order in $s$, keeping a product only where one
factor does not vanish in value, is valid for the gradient but, by
[(33)](#eq-s-squared), not for the Hessian.

Reversed this way, the shift receives a contribution from every
assignment in which it occurs, including two from evaluating $f_{e}$
and $f_{a}$ at $t^{*}$, which depends on $\theta$:
[]{#eq-shift-clock}
$$
  \bar s \;\supset\;
    \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\right)_{\!(x_{a}, t^{*})}\!\!\cdot \bar f_{a}
    + \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\right)_{\!(x_{e}, t^{*})}\!\!\cdot \bar f_{e} . \tag{40}
$$
Both cotangents contain a factor $s$, so [(40)](#eq-shift-clock) is absent
from the gradient and enters the Hessian at full strength. It vanishes
identically for an autonomous right-hand side; a pruned form omits it
whenever $\partial f/\partial t \neq 0$.

The forward path corrects the shift by
$-\tfrac{1}{2}(\ddot g / \dot g)\,s^{2}$, whose chain factor
$1 + 2 c_{2} s$, $c_{2} = -\ddot g / (2\dot g)$, is one in value and a
second-order tangent; the transpose applies it to
$\partial s / \partial x$.

The sweep binds the tangent storage of every buffer it hands to a
generated contraction (see [forward over reverse](methods-forward-reverse.html)). In the jump transpose
every read of such a buffer is multiplied by $s$, so an unbound buffer
would leave value and gradient intact and make the Hessian wrong by a
rank-one term.

**Derivative of the shift.** Since $\dot g$ depends on the state,
[]{#eq-root-quotient}
$$
  \frac{\partial s}{\partial x}
    = -\frac{\nabla g}{\dot g} - \frac{s}{\dot g}\, \nabla \dot g ,
  \qquad
  \nabla \dot g = \nabla \frac{\partial g}{\partial t}
                + \left(\nabla^{2} g\right) f + J^{\mathsf T}\nabla g , \tag{41}
$$
and the second term contains $g$, which is zero in value: absent from
the gradient, full strength in the Hessian. The generator differentiates
$\dot g = \partial g/\partial t + \nabla g \cdot f$ as one expression
rather than assembling three terms, so all three are present, including the
two that vanish for a $g$ linear in the state and independent of time.
This yields
$\nabla \partial g/\partial t$ and $(\nabla^{2} g) f$ and, on $\theta$,
the matching $\partial^{2} g/\partial\theta\,\partial t$,
$(\partial \nabla g/\partial\theta)\cdot f$ and
$(\partial f/\partial\theta)^{\mathsf T}\nabla g$. A forcing inside $g$
is differentiated in $t$ through its rate: the time derivative on the
expression graph seeds each forcing leaf with a rate leaf, which prints
as the derivative of the PCHIP interpolant.

**Time-dependent resets.** A reset value $h$ that depends
explicitly on time is applied on the surface, at $t^{*}$, so
[]{#eq-reset-clock}
$$
  \frac{\partial x_{a}}{\partial t^{*}} \;\supset\; c\,
  \frac{\partial h}{\partial t}, \qquad
  c = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{add} \\ 1 & \text{replace} \\ x_{\ast k} &
  \text{multiply,}\end{cases} \tag{42}
$$
which contributes to $\kappa$ of [(31)](#eq-saltation-adjoint). This
term is first order: omitting it makes the gradient wrong, not only the
Hessian. For the same reason the transposed reset receives the event
time as a dual rather than a plain number, so that
$\partial h/\partial\theta$ includes the dependence of $t^{*}$ on
$\theta$. Such a value evaluates $t^{*}$ directly and inherits the root
tolerance rather than the integration tolerance; in a value that
depends only on the state at $t^{*}$ the localisation error is damped
by the smoothness of the trajectory.

**Verification.** With $R = \mathrm{id}$ the composition
[(39)](#eq-root-sandwich) is the identity and the transpose cancels term
by term. Against a nested-dual evaluation of the same sandwich, without
solver, store or event engine, the transpose is exact to
$9\cdot10^{-16}$. Over a whole trajectory, compared with forward over
forward on one recorded step sequence, the second order agrees to the
tolerance of the solve. Only this last check is sensitive to
[(40)](#eq-shift-clock): the nested-dual check compares against the same
forward routine the transpose reverses, so a term absent from both
sides cancels.

## Verifying a derivative across a moving event

When $t^{*}$ depends on a parameter, the reported trajectory contains a
row whose time moves with it. A functional $w^{\mathsf T} x$ seeded on
that row differs between parameter values and has no derivative to
compare against. Restricting the cotangent to the user's own output
times restores a well-posed functional, and the forward,
forward-over-forward and difference-quotient answers then agree to the
tolerance of the solve.

## Internal numerical differentiation

The step sizes the controller selected are constants of the
differentiated map. This is Bock's internal numerical differentiation
[@bock1981numerical; @albersmeyer2010adjoint]: the nominal run adapts freely, and the derivative is taken of the
scheme that run applied. Differentiating the control law instead adds
derivatives of the step sizes to the chain rule and makes the discrete
adjoint inconsistent with the adjoint ODE
[@eberhard1999automatic; @alexe2009discrete]; that term, measured at
$O(\text{tol})$, is left out.

The usual justification, that $h$ is piecewise constant in $\theta$
with zero derivative almost everywhere, does not hold for an adaptive
controller, and the argument below does not rely on it. Let
$y_{h}(\theta)$ be the result the program returns on the grid the
controller selects at $\theta$. Then
[]{#eq-grid-effect}
$$
  \frac{\mathrm{d} y_{h}}{\mathrm{d}\theta}
    = \frac{\partial y_{h}}{\partial \theta}
    + \sum_{k} \frac{\partial y_{h}}{\partial h_{k}}\,
      \frac{\mathrm{d} h_{k}}{\mathrm{d}\theta} , \tag{43}
$$
where internal numerical differentiation computes the first term and
the sum is the grid effect, which differentiating the control law would
add.

The step size $h(\theta)$ is piecewise smooth with jumps: within an
acceptance region it varies smoothly through the error estimate, and at
its boundary an accepted step is rejected and the entire later grid
shifts. Halving the spacing of a sweep in $\theta$ doubles the measured
magnitude of the grid effect, which identifies it as a jump height
divided by $\Delta\theta$, not a derivative. Automatic differentiation
reproduces only the smooth part, so differentiating the control law
returns the exact gradient plus the smooth part of the grid effect,
without the jump part, which is the larger of the two. The result is
neither the derivative of the exact solution, to which the addition
does not belong, nor that of the reported value, whose dominant
contribution is missing. Recovering the grid effect requires a smoothed
controller, a fixed grid or a randomised estimator, none of which
differentiating the existing chain provides.

Each mode returns the state it integrated together with the derivative
of the scheme that produced it, so both follow internal numerical
differentiation for the solve they answer. The grids differ from that
of a value run in the forward mode: with the default
`sensErrCon = TRUE` it maximises its error norm over the
sensitivity columns as in [(15)](methods-forward.html#eq-wrms-sens), integrates on a grid
finer than a value run takes, and its values differ from a value run's by
$O(\mathrm{tol})$. The default keeps the sensitivities in the error norm
because they are integrated alongside the state and their errors
accumulate; CVODES guards against this in the same way
(`CVodeSetSensErrCon`). The value pass of the reverse mode takes the
grid of a value run, as the forward run of CVODES' adjoint sensitivity
analysis does, and the reverse gradient is the derivative of the trajectory
a value run returns.

## Why the state error is not enough

A grid selected from the state error alone need not resolve the
linearised flow. The derivative of the step map is accurate where the
step resolves the flow on the modes present in the tangents, and the
state error measures that only on the modes present in the state,
weighted by its own magnitude. On a trajectory at rest it measures
nothing: a state that starts at zero and is not driven, or a steady
state, is a polynomial the corrector reproduces, its error estimate is
zero, and the step grows by the controller's maximum factor on every step.
The adjoint on that grid is the exact derivative of a scheme far from
the flow. For $\dot x = -k x$, $\dot y = k x - y$ from $x = y = 0$ over
$0, 1, \ldots, 50$, a grid of four steps returns $+0.80$ for a
contraction whose value is $-0.43$. Internal numerical differentiation
meets the same failure for $\dot x = p x$ from $x = 0$
[@albersmeyer2010adjoint, Sec. 6.7.5], and forward automatic
differentiation through an adaptive solver meets it unless the
controller's norm includes the derivative parts
[@sapienza2024differentiable]. Where a state is small against
$\mathtt{abstol}/\mathtt{reltol}$ the effect is weaker but of the same
kind. A parameter can also reach the flow where the state does not see
it: in $\dot x = -k x + \sin(100 t)\, q$ at $q = 0$ the state is smooth
while $\partial x/\partial q$ follows the fast forcing, and a parameter
that enters only through an event's value acts on the flow from that
event on. Such a gradient is resolved by [checking the sweep](#refine), not the value pass.

## Checking the sweep {#refine}

`adjointControl(refine = TRUE)` holds the sweep to the tolerances,
step by step, on the trajectory the value pass stored. It applies the local
error test of the backward problem of CVODES [@serban2005cvodes], so that a
tolerance means the same for both. Step $n$ hands $\lambda(t_n)$ to the step
below and adds a share $\Delta\bar\theta_n$ to the parameter gradient, whose
sum from the end of the run down to $t_n$ is the running gradient
$\bar\theta(t_n)$. With $\delta$ the error estimate of the step's adjoint,
the step passes when
[]{#eq-refine-test}
$$
  \begin{gathered}
  \max\Bigl(\bigl\|\delta\lambda(t_n)\bigr\|_{\mathrm{rms},\,w_\lambda},\;
             \bigl\|\delta\Delta\bar\theta_n\bigr\|_{\mathrm{rms},\,w_\theta}\Bigr) \le 1,
  \\
  w_{\lambda,i} = \mathtt{reltol}\,|\lambda_i(t_n)| + \mathtt{abstol},
  \qquad
  w_{\theta,i} = \mathtt{reltol}\,|\bar\theta_i(t_n)| + \mathtt{gradtol},
  \end{gathered} \tag{44}
$$
in the weighted root-mean-square norm of [(10)](methods-stepping.html#eq-wrms). The gradient term
enters only with `gradtol`, as CVODES holds its quadrature to the
error test only with an absolute tolerance on it
(`CVodeSetQuadErrConB`). The test is local: the errors of the steps
add up over the sweep, as the forward mode's do over the run.

**The estimate.** Under `rb4` the step's output is $X_6 + e$ and
its embedded solution $X_6$, so the adjoints of the two differ by the
response to a seed on $e$ alone. That response is one more backward pass
over the same stages and the same factorisation, and estimates the error
of the embedded adjoint. A step that meets [(44)](#eq-refine-test) with it
is taken as it is. Otherwise the step is taken again in $m = 2, 4,
\ldots, 1024$ substeps from its own start state, forward and back with the
observations that fall into each, and successive refinements are
compared. The difference $d_m$ is divided by Richardson's factor
$\min\bigl(2^q - 1,\; \max(1,\, d_{m/2}/d_m - 1)\bigr)$ only as far as two successive
differences show the order $q$; the first halving is taken at face
value. `tsit5` has no embedded adjoint and starts with the halving.
With `adjointControl(trace = TRUE)`, `$adjoint$substeps`
reports the $m$ each step took.

**Multistep methods.** The share of a `bdf` or `adams` step
cannot be recomputed in halves: the Nordsieck array couples the step to
the history before it at order one, and replacing one step by substeps
changes what every later step reads. The checked sweep integrates the
flow's adjoint between the grid points instead, each interval from the
stored start state, and hands only the state cotangent across a grid
point. Its gradient is the derivative of the flow along the computed
trajectory, not of the scheme, and differs from the scheme's derivative
by the order of the tolerance, as the continuous adjoint of CVODES does
[@serban2005cvodes].

The flow over an interval of length $H$ is extrapolated linearly implicit
Euler, the scheme of SEULEX [@hairer2010solving, §IV.9]. Chain $j$
takes $n_j = j$ steps of $h_j = H/n_j$,
[]{#eq-lie-chain}
$$
  \bigl(h_j^{-1} I - J_0\bigr)\, D_k = f(x_k, t_k), \qquad x_{k+1} = x_k + D_k, \tag{45}
$$
on the one Jacobian $J_0$ at the interval's start. A chain is a W-method:
it is consistent for any matrix in place of the Jacobian, so its error has
an expansion in powers of $h_j$, and the Aitken-Neville tableau
$T_{j,k} = T_{j,k-1} + (T_{j,k-1} - T_{j-1,k-1}) / (n_j/n_{j-k} - 1)$
raises the order by one per column. Chain $j$ costs one factorisation of
$h_j^{-1} I - J_0$, a change of the diagonal of one Jacobian, $n_j$
right-hand sides and $n_j$ solves.

The extrapolated state $T_{j,j}$ is a fixed linear combination of the
chains' end states, so its adjoint is the same combination of the chains'
adjoints, and the tableau is built on those: the cotangent of the start
state and the interval's share of the gradient, each chain swept back on
its own factorisation. A step of [(45)](#eq-lie-chain) hands
$\mu_k = (h_j^{-1} I - J_0)^{-\mathsf T} \lambda_{k+1}$ to $x_k$ through
$J(x_k)^{\mathsf T} \mu_k$ and to $\theta$ through
$f_\theta(x_k)^{\mathsf T} \mu_k$, and through $J_0$ to the interval's
start: $\sum_k \mu_k^{\mathsf T} (\partial J_0)\, D_k$ is one bilinear
form over the Jacobian's pattern, $M_{rc} = \sum_k \mu_{k,r} D_{k,c}$,
which the generated code pulls back in one evaluation. The difference
$e_j$ of two neighbouring entries $T_{j,j}$, $T_{j,j-1}$ estimates the
error of $T_{j,j-1}$; $T_{j,j}$ is returned, and its error is estimated as
$e_j \min(1, e_j/e_{j-1})$, the rate of the last two differences applied
one column on, as CVODES estimates the error of the solution it returns.
The first column whose estimate passes [(44)](#eq-refine-test) is taken,
and an interval the eighth does not pass is halved, its midpoint reached forward under the state's
own test. An observation inside the interval cuts it there, the piece
after it starting from the state the state's own test reaches.

**Limits.** A one-step method's step that misses the test at 1024
substeps is taken with 1024, and the halving stops early where from
$m = 32$ on a halving no longer shrinks the difference; a multistep
interval is halved at most ten times. An error source that the
refinement does not reduce, a forcing far faster than the steps, leaves
the estimate below the error.

## Relation to the forward mode

Forward and reverse derivatives of the same model do not agree to
machine precision: the two modes differentiate different discretisations,
each exactly, or under `refine` the reverse mode the flow, and the
difference falls with the tolerance. The value and the reverse gradient
returned to the caller are consistent, which a trust-region method,
comparing a predicted with an achieved reduction, relies on.

Of the implicit methods, the Rosenbrock adjoint is the most accurate: its
stages are direct solves, so its adjoint is the exact transpose of the
discrete step, whereas the adjoint of a corrector applies the implicit
function theorem to an iteration stopped at a finite tolerance.

The reverse mode supports all four methods, time- and root-triggered
events, forcings, the batch entry point and the sparse linear solver.
It is implemented in `cppde_adjoint_step.hpp`,
`cppde_reverse_step.hpp` and
`cppde_reverse_trajectory.hpp`.
